# CHAPTER XII:

ECCENTRICITY (1863)

Knowledge of human nature is the beginning and end of political education, but several years of arduous study in the neighborhood of Westminster led Henry Adams to think that knowledge of English human nature had little or no value outside of England. The English mind was one-sided, eccentric, systematically unsystematic, and logically illogical. The less one knew of it, the better.

For several years he observed the English mind in contact with itself and other minds. The commonest phrase overheard at an English club or dinner-table was that So-and-So "is quite mad." It was no offence; it hardly distinguished him from his fellows. Eccentricity was so general as to become hereditary distinction. It made the chief charm of English society as well as its chief terror.

Often this eccentricity bore all the marks of strength; perhaps it was actual exuberance of force, a birthmark of genius. Boston thought so. The Bostonian called it national character—native vigor—robustness—honesty—courage. He respected and feared it. But the cleverest Englishmen held that the national eccentricity needed correction, and were beginning to correct it.

The private secretary, like every other Bostonian, began by regarding British eccentricity as a force. Contact with Palmerston, Russell, and Gladstone made him hesitate; he saw his own national type deal with the British and show itself certainly not the weaker. Russell might be dishonest or merely obtuse—the English type might be brutal or only stupid—but strong, in either case, it was not, nor did it seem strong to Englishmen.

By natural affinity the social eccentrics sympathized with political eccentricity. The English mind took naturally to rebellion—when foreign—and felt particular confidence in the Southern Confederacy, which combined every ideal eccentricity. All the English eccentrics rushed into the ranks of rebel sympathizers; the "cranks" were all rebels, and the list was portentous.

This eccentricity did not mean strength. The proof lay in the mismanagement of the rebel interests. No one understood why Jefferson Davis chose Mr. Mason as his agent for London. Mason became Mr. Adams's bulwark of defence: he had his usual luck in enemies, who were always his most valuable allies if his friends only let them alone.

Never was there a moment when eccentricity, if it were a force, should have had more value to the rebel interest; and the managers adopted as their champion an eccentric of eccentrics: Mr. Roebuck, once tribune of the people, who in growing old had grown fatuous. The Minister sent his private secretary down to the House of Commons on June 30, 1863, to report the result of Roebuck's motion to recognize the Southern Confederacy. The Legation felt no anxiety, having Vicksburg already in its pocket. He listened, with great content, while John Bright, with astonishing force, caught and shook and tossed Roebuck, as a big mastiff shakes a wiry, ill-conditioned, toothless, bad-tempered Yorkshire terrier.

All the more sharply was he excited, near the year 1879 in Washington, by hearing Lamar begin a story after dinner which little by little became dramatic, recalling the scene from the other side. Before the debate, at Lindsay's villa on the Thames, Lamar had bethought himself of John Bright and asked Roebuck whether he expected him to take part.

"No, sir!" said Roebuck sententiously. "Bright and I have met before. It was the old story—the story of the sword-fish and the whale! NO, sir! Mr. Bright will not cross swords with me again!"

Thus assured, Lamar went with the more confidence to the House, and followed the debate with the enjoyment of an experienced debater, until, as he said, he became aware that a man, with a singularly rich voice and imposing manner, had taken the floor, and was giving Roebuck the most deliberate and tremendous pounding he ever witnessed, "until at last," concluded Lamar, "it dawned on my mind that the sword-fish was getting the worst of it."

Such jokes must have been unpleasantly common in the experience of the rebel agents. Extreme eccentricity was no bar, in England, to extreme confidence; sometimes it seemed a recommendation.

Bright's own courage was almost as irrational as that of the rebels themselves. He struck, in succession, pretty nearly every man in England that could be reached by a blow, and when he could not reach the individual he struck the class. He was a liberal hater, and what he hated he reviled after the manner of Milton, but he was afraid of no one. To an American he seemed more English than any of his critics—singularly well poised, yet using singularly strong language.
